channel.title: llunatic-lab (en)
channel.description: Security notes from the dark side of the internet

item.title: Codex Security CLI: OpenAI's Open-Source Scanner That Finds, Validates, and Fixes Bugs
item.description: OpenAI's codex-security CLI scans your repo, argues with its own findings until only the real ones survive, then drafts the patch and re-checks it. Version 0.10.0 just made it resumable, budget-capped, and CI-ready — here's how to run it, and the two catches nobody should skip.

item.title: Passkeys: The Credential That Can't Be Phished — and Why November 2026 Is the Tipping Point
item.description: Passwords are a shared secret, so they can be phished, guessed, and leaked. Passkeys replace them with a private key that never leaves your device — and in November 2026, Microsoft made them the first step of sign-in, not an optional extra.

item.title: Apache mod_http2 RCE (CVE-2026-119618): Check Your Server, Kill HTTP/2, Patch to 2.4.71
item.description: Apache 2.4.71 fixes a critical heap-corruption flaw in mod_http2 that can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution — and Wiz found 64% of cloud environments exposed. This walkthrough shows you how to check whether your server is affected, disable HTTP/2 as a stopgap, and patch properly.

item.title: Able2Shell: How 33 Zero-Days Took N-central Offline — and the Patch That Didn't Hold
item.description: On a Sunday in November, one researcher published 33 zero-days in N-able's N-central with working exploits. By Monday the platform was offline worldwide; by Thursday, cryptominers were running on patched servers. This is the anatomy of a disclosure that broke every rule — and the week that followed.

item.title: Audit Your Own Repos for Leaked Secrets: A Hands-On Gitleaks and TruffleHog Walkthrough
item.description: GitGuardian counted 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets on public GitHub in 2025, and attackers now go from a leaked key to a drained cloud vault in five minutes. This walkthrough sets up Gitleaks and TruffleHog on your own repos — scan the history, block the next leak at commit time, and know exactly what to rotate when one slips through.

item.title: sshole: The OpenSSH Bug That Logs You Into Accounts With No Password
item.description: On November 5, OpenSSH shipped an emergency fix for CVE-2026-123158 — a logic bug that lets anyone log into a passwordless account on Alpine Linux with a password nobody set. The first exploitation attempts arrived within nine hours.

item.title: One Guarantor, 189 Banks: The SMBC Consumer Finance Breach
item.description: You never opened an account with SMBC Consumer Finance — but if you took a card loan from one of 189 Japanese banks, your name, income, and driver's license number may have sat in its guarantee system. On November 2, an intruder walked out with records on up to 320,118 people.

item.title: Turn Your Coding Agent Into a Security Auditor: Inside Cloudflare's Security-Audit Skill
item.description: Cloudflare open-sourced the skill that seeded its fleet-wide vulnerability discovery harness: a six-phase audit workflow where a fresh agent tries to disprove every finding before it counts. Here's how it works, what it costs, and the sandbox rule you must not skip.

item.title: When the Editor Is the Exploit: Why an Unauthenticated Admin Panel Is Already Remote Code Execution
item.description: Node-RED's editor lets anyone who can reach it write and run code — by design. When Siemens disclosed CVE-2026-58115 in August 2026, attackers needed no exploit chain, no stolen password, and no malware trick: the editor itself was the exploit, and by October 30 it was being used in the wild.

item.title: Patched on Paper, Vulnerable in Production: A Hands-On Node2Shell Audit
item.description: Node.js fixed Node2Shell on October 21, but the version string lies, the runtime hides in containers, and npm update does nothing. This audit walks you through proving — not assuming — that every Node.js in your estate is actually patched.

item.title: Patched, Upgraded — Still Vulnerable: The GitLab Flaw That Hid in Ruby
item.description: Alpine Linux upgraded its GitLab twice and stayed vulnerable both times, because the CVSS 10.0 flaw CVE-2026-97229 lived not in GitLab's code but in the Ruby interpreter underneath it. Here is the timeline, the trap, and how to check your own instance.

item.title: Installed but Never Imported — and It Still Stole Your Keys: Hunting the LiteLLM .pth Stealer
item.description: On October 21, 2026, a poisoned LiteLLM 1.107.0 release hid a credential stealer in a Python startup file — so it ran in every Python process on the host, even ones that never touched LiteLLM. Here is how to check whether it touched you, and how to clean it up properly.

item.title: Patch by Exploitation, Not by Score: How CISA's KEV Catalog Reorders Your Queue
item.description: A CVSS 10.0 flaw with no known exploitation and a CVSS 8.8 flaw attackers are already using — which do you patch first? October 2026 gave that question a very expensive answer, and CISA's KEV catalog is how smart teams stop getting it wrong.

item.title: The Invisible Sticker That Guards Windows: A Hands-On Mark of the Web Lab
item.description: CVE-2026-96951, exploited in the wild, strips the invisible tag Windows puts on internet downloads — and with it, SmartScreen, Protected View, and the macro block all go quiet. This lab shows you how to see that tag, test what it controls, and hunt files that lost it.

item.title: Read-Only to Superuser: Arista's VeloCloud Zero-Day and the Third Strike on SD-WAN's Control Plane
item.description: Arista's October 22 advisory describes a SQL injection flaw that turns the lowest-privilege VeloCloud account into a full operator — the third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator flaw since July, and the first that only needs a login.

item.title: PHP2Shell: When the Runtime Itself Is the Vulnerability — A Case Breakdown
item.description: No plugin was broken. No password was guessed. Two flaws in PHP itself let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a web server — and the first exploit attempts arrived four days before the patch existed.

item.title: Zeabur: How Plaintext Secrets Killed a Hosting Platform — A Case Breakdown
item.description: No zero-day. No nation-state. Just a non-expiring admin token sitting in plaintext in a config repo — and it cost Zeabur 3.2 million secrets, root on 101 customer servers, and eventually the company itself.

item.title: Your Agent's Plugins Are the New Attack Surface: Auditing MCP Servers With mcp-scan
item.description: AI agents now browse the web, run code, and query databases through MCP servers — and attackers have noticed. Here's how tool poisoning works, why October 2026 turned MCP into a headline threat, and how to audit your own setup with Invariant Labs' mcp-scan before a plugin audits you.

item.title: From PoC to Detection in Minutes: Your First Nuclei Template
item.description: When a critical CVE drops, exploit PoCs hit GitHub within hours — and mass scanning follows. Nuclei lets you scan your own estate just as fast by turning a proof of concept into a shareable YAML template. Here's how the tool works, how to write your first template, and the guardrails that keep it from burning you.

item.title: Double Extortion: How Modern Ransomware Really Works
item.description: Modern ransomware doesn't care about your backups — attackers steal your data first, then encrypt it, then squeeze you from three directions at once. Here's the full playbook, from initial access to the leak site, grounded in the October 2026 Semperis report and this month's real cases.
